chapter_theme: The opening of Pattinathar's lament spoken as a woman to her friend: she bowed to Ganesa asking for grace, and one came, showed his form and took the guru's shape, then burned everything she was made of: the six centres and fifty-one letters, the elements, the senses, the instruments of mind, the three tiers of tattvas and the ninety-six, the stone fort of the body, Om itself and the ego, and both deeds. What is left is a woman alone who knows herself, a house with no one in it, open space, and a town that laughs at her.
structure_note: The whole work is in the second person feminine (மகடூ முன்னிலை): every line ends in -அடி (the friend) or -ஆண்டி (he did, girl), and 'he' is the guru-Lord who came as a man. 506 to 509 and 513 are near-doublets of Azhuganni 33 to 36, so the same cipher of a burned fort is shared between the two laments. The verses run in waves: the burning of the body's constituents (508 to 517, 521 to 525), a question about who he was (518 to 520), the cutting of deeds and the knowing of self (526 to 528), and the public aftermath (529, 530). The first four units carry PARALLELS to Azhuganni; the chapter has no glosses or variant notes.

506.reading: I bowed to the five-handed god asking to receive grace; and one came without delay and showed me his own form.
506.nuance: ஐங்கரன் (the five-handed) is Ganesa, so the work opens with the usual invocation, but here the invocation is already the story: the prayer is answered by a man who arrives. தன்சொரூபம் is his form; the Azhuganni doublet reads தற்சொரூபம், the form of the self, and the two readings differ in whether what she was shown was him or herself.

507.reading: To cut off the plundering birth he took the guru's form; to cut off the thieving senses he came as the cause.
507.nuance: கொள்ளைப் பிறப்பு and கள்ளப் புலன் pair birth and the senses as robbers. குருவடிவம் கொண்டான் says the guru's shape is taken on, not that he is one; the Siddhars' guru is the Lord in a body.

508.reading: The six supports and the fifty-one letters, the whole fort of deceit, he burned so that no fault remained.
508.nuance: ஆதாரம் ஓராறு are the six centres of the yogic body and ஐம்பத்தோர் அட்சரம் the fifty-one letters that tradition distributes over them. The fort (கோட்டை) is the body, as in the Meynjanap-pulambal's காயாபுரிக்கோட்டை. The surprise is that the very apparatus of yoga is what he burns; the verse does not say he used it.

509.reading: The many, many tattvas that breed so much disturbance all lost their heads and burned.
509.nuance: விகாரம் is change or disturbance; the tattvas are blamed as its source. தலைகெட்டு, losing their heads, is both ruin and the end of their rule.

510.reading: All those born together with me have died; I cannot stay all alone by myself.
510.nuance: Plainly a woman mourning her siblings; in the cipher of 508 and 509 those born with her are the faculties and elements that came with the body, which the burning has killed. The complaint that she cannot bear to be alone is answered at 528, where being alone is the ripeness.

511.reading: Saying 'this is the field where everyone fell', I would perish; if I speak and weep, when will my sorrow abate?
511.nuance: பட்டகளம் is a battlefield after the slaughter, the body or world after the burning. தொலையுமடி may be 'I would be done for' or 'it would end'; the question of the second line is not answered.

512.reading: I saw the five elements beginning with earth die and fall; I saw the five senses beginning with the sky-born burn and fall.
512.nuance: விண்முதலாம் ஐம்பொறி makes the senses begin from the sky, since hearing is the sense of the ether; the two lines run the elements up and the senses down.

513.reading: The five unparting waters burned to ash; I saw the five beginning with speech die and fall.
513.nuance: வாக்காதி ஐவர் are the five organs of action (speech, hands, feet, excretion, generation) of the tattva lists. நீங்காப் புனல் ஐந்து is unclear: perhaps the five fluids of the body, or the five senses as a flood that never leaves; the Azhuganni doublet lacks the line.

514.reading: All the instruments of mind perished, each in its kind, and burned and fell together with their kindred instruments.
514.nuance: மனக்கரணம் are the inner instruments (mind, intellect, memory, ego); இனக்கரணம், their kin, are the outer senses and organs as tradition reads it. The verse does not list them.

515.reading: The soul's tattvas burned, their tiers destroyed; how could one praise him, who has taken my awareness away?
515.nuance: ஆத்தும தத்துவம் is the first of the three tiers of the thirty-six (the twenty-four atma tattvas), and 516 follows with the vidya tattvas and the five pure ones, so 515 to 517 walk the Siddhanta scheme. போதமிழந்தானை can be 'him who lost awareness' or, as taken here, 'him by whom awareness was lost'; the reading turns on it.

516.reading: I saw the vidya tattvas burn and fall; he burned the five pure ones too, so that no fault remained.
516.nuance: சுத்தவித்தை ஐந்து are the five siva tattvas of the pure order, the highest of the thirty-six. Even these burn; the refrain துரிசறவே (fault gone) returns from 508.

517.reading: The branches of three kinds and the thirty-six he burned till they spat and fell, and cut the root of the womb.
517.nuance: முப்பத்தறுவர் are the thirty-six tattvas just enumerated. மூன்று வகைக் கிளை is not explained: the three tiers of 515 and 516, or the three malas, or the three gunas. கருவேர் அறுத்தல், cutting the root of the embryo, is ending rebirth, and recurs at 523 and 532.

518.reading: Did he come as a guru, or to destroy my clan? Did he come as a form, or to destroy form?
518.nuance: Four questions with the same shape. குலம் is caste or family, so the plain sense is a girl ruined for her people; it is also the lineage of births. The last question is the Saiva paradox of a Lord who takes form to end form, and 576 sees him lose his form.

519.reading: I did not know ruin would come; I did not know, blind to my ruined wit, that suffering would come; I stayed with the Lord ruling me.
519.nuance: பதி ஆண்டு இருந்தேன் is read as 'I remained, the Lord having taken me'; பதி can also be a town, giving 'I stayed in the place'. கெடுமதி, the wit that is ruined, is what she did not see; the ruin she laments is the one she asked for at 506.

520.reading: I did not know this was the field where everyone fell; I saw the one without senses, who ends all evil.
520.nuance: பொறியிலி is taken as the one without sense organs, the Lord beyond the senses that 507 cut off; பொறி also means a trap and luck, and 'the luckless one' is a possible self-mockery. பட்டகளம் returns from 511.

521.reading: Those within the inner fort all died together; those within that fort, sixty of them, fell.
521.nuance: அறுபது பேர், the sixty, with the thirty-six of 517 make the ninety-six of 523, the Tamil count of the body's constituents; that is how tradition reconciles the numbers, and the verse does not. உட்கோட்டை and அக்கோட்டை may be two forts or the same one.

522.reading: They died together; it burned right through; the whole stone fort became a fort of charcoal.
522.nuance: கற்கோட்டை to கரிக்கோட்டை is the body as a fortress reduced to its own cinders; the verse is the chapter's picture in a single rhyme.

523.reading: He burned the ninety-six so that no fault remained; the evil eye struck, and he cut the root of the womb.
523.nuance: தொண்ணூற்றறுவர் are the ninety-six tattvas of the Tamil count. கண்ணேறு is the evil eye, the glance that blights; here it is his glance that blighted her, and tradition hears in it the guru's initiating look (நயன தீட்சை). The text has துரிசறிவே for the refrain துரிசறவே.

524.reading: Om was ruined, all that is went; the ego was ruined, he cut it off at the root.
524.nuance: ஓங்காரம் and ஆங்காரம் are paired by rhyme and fall together: the highest mantra goes with the lowest fault. உள்ளதெல்லாம் போச்சு, 'everything that was went', leaves the void the next chapters stand in.

525.reading: From the earth-hut upward it burned right through; he cut off every trouble of the roaring mind.
525.nuance: தரையாங் குடிலை is read plainly as the hut that is earth, the body; but குடிலை is also the Tamil name for the pure maya (kutila) at the top of the tattva scale, which gives 'from earth to kutilai', the whole range from lowest to highest. The coded reading fits 515 to 517 better.

526.reading: He cut off all my former deeds entirely, and so that I might know myself I became one woman alone.
526.nuance: தான் ஒருத்தி ஆனேன், 'I became a single woman', turns the loneliness of 510 into self-knowledge; தன்னை அறிய is the refrain of 526 to 528.

527.reading: So that I might know myself he destroyed both deeds to their foundation, and told me the place where I could know myself.
527.nuance: இருவினை are good and bad karma. தலம் is a place, perhaps the seat in the body or the state; the verse says he told it and does not tell it.

528.reading: I knew myself; I became a maiden by myself; is this the ripeness, to stay all alone, utterly alone?
528.nuance: தனிக்குமரி, the lone maiden, after the loss of maidenhood in 531 and 574: the one who was taken is a virgin again, with no other. பக்குவமோ can be a doubt or a wondering assent.

529.reading: There is no one in the house; I became open space; all I saw turned into a dream, like moonlight cast on a forest.
529.nuance: வெட்டவெளி, the open expanse, is the Siddhars' word for the state beyond the tattvas. காட்டுக்கு எறித்த நிலா is proverbial for a light wasted on no one; here it may be all she saw, now worthless, or the light that now shines in an emptied place.

530.reading: Will those who see not laugh? Is it not a song for the whole country? Will those who see not turn hostile? Is it not talk for those who look?
530.nuance: The chapter ends in the love-poetry convention of town gossip (அலர): a girl whose state is visible becomes a song and a scandal. For the Siddhar the jnani's condition is likewise what the world laughs at.

links.note: The same verse as Azhuganni 33 with the ஆத்தாடி refrain: the bow to Ganesa and the one who came and showed his form. The Azhuganni reads தற்சொரூபம், the self's form, where this reads தன்சொரூபம், his own.

Both say the grace that frees comes in the guru's form: Tirumular's grace-power comes as the guru when the two deeds balance; Pattinathar's Lord took the guru's shape to cut birth and the senses, and 527 has him destroying the two deeds.
The body as a fort: the Meynjanap-pulambal asks when it will seize the fort of the body-city; here the fort of deceit, with its six centres and fifty-one letters, is burned down.
Azhuganni 35 is the same couplet with the refrain; both burn the six supports and the fifty-one letters as a deceitful fort.
Azhuganni 36 combines this line on the tattvas losing their heads with the line on the five beginning with speech that appears here at 513.

Both have the guru take the disciple past the thirty-six: Nandi makes their nature known and then stands beyond them; Pattinathar's guru burns them and cuts the root of birth. Tirumular keeps the tattvas as something learned; Pattinathar only destroys them.

Tirumular's ninety-six (thirty, thirty and thirty-six) live in a walled temple and run off when it falls; Pattinathar's sixty die inside the fort when it burns. In Tirumular the constituents outlive the body; here they are killed with it.
The Kural says cutting off the pride that says 'I' and 'mine' enters the highest world; Pattinathar's guru cuts the ego (ஆங்காரம்) at the root. Pattinathar adds that Om itself goes with it.

Tirumular faults those in whom the light of Om rises but who never gain the ego-free experience; Pattinathar goes a step further and has Om and ego ruined together, so that even the pranava is not kept.
In the first part of the lament (முதல்வன் முறையீடு) the poet asks whether the open space that ends burning sorrow will not come to him; here, in the woman's voice, he says he has become it.
Bhadragiriyar asks when he will see clearly the bare void grown in the open space; Pattinathar's speaker has become the open space and sees everything else as a dream.

In the Kural the town, not knowing the woman's worth, makes the lover a present of gossip; Pattinathar's speaker, whose state is now visible, expects to be the country's song and the lookers' talk. The lover's gossip becomes the jnani's.

source_issues: 523 line 1 reads துரிசறிவே where 508 and 516 have the refrain துரிசறவே; probably a copying slip.

506 to 509 and 513 are near-doublets of Azhuganni 33 to 36 (seq 1521 to 1524), and the corpus records the PARALLELS; the attribution of the shared lines to Pattinathar or to the Azhuganni's author is open.
